Jun had lived on Maple Street for only two weeks, and he did not know anyone in his new neighborhood yet. Every afternoon, he sat on the front steps and watched the cars go by while he thought about his old friends and his old school.

Next door lived an older woman named Mrs. Ortiz, who spent every afternoon working in her backyard garden. One afternoon she waved at Jun over the fence. "I could use some help," she called. "My tomato plants are thirsty, and my back is tired."

Jun shrugged, but he walked over to her yard anyway. Mrs. Ortiz handed him a green watering can and showed him how to pour the water slowly at the bottom of each plant. "Roots drink better when you are gentle," she explained.

The plants were tall, but the tomatoes were still small, hard, and green. "When will they be ready?" Jun asked.

"Not today," Mrs. Ortiz answered with a gentle smile, "but good things take time."

After that, Jun came over every afternoon. He pulled weeds and tied the long stems to wooden sticks so they would not bend. Some days were very hot, and he wanted to quit, but he kept coming back because he liked to hear Mrs. Ortiz tell stories about the garden she had as a girl.

Slowly, the tomatoes grew bigger, and then one morning, Jun noticed a flash of red and ran to the fence. "Mrs. Ortiz! The first one is ripe!" They picked it together, and it tasted sweet and delicious.

Soon there were too many tomatoes for one person to eat. Mrs. Ortiz filled a basket with tomatoes and gave it to Jun. "Share these with your class," she said. "You helped grow them."

The next day, Jun carried the basket to school, and his teacher let him tell the class about the garden. A girl named Lily raised her hand. "Can you show me how to grow tomatoes?" she asked. "I want to plant some too."

Jun grinned. "Sure," he said, "but you have to be patient. Good things take time."

That afternoon, Jun did not sit alone on the steps, because he and Lily walked to the garden next door together. Jun thought about how lonely he had felt just a few weeks before. Now he had a garden, a teacher next door, and a brand-new friend.
stem: What is the main lesson of this story?
choices: Being patient and helping others can lead to good things, like new friends.
It is better to stay home than to go to a new school.
Tomatoes are the easiest plants to grow in a garden.
You should never talk to your neighbors.
explanation: Jun is patient in the garden and helps Mrs. Ortiz, and this leads to sharing tomatoes and making a new friend, Lily.

Long ago, a tired traveler walked into a small village at the end of a cold day. He carried only a walking stick, a big iron pot, and a smooth gray stone, and he was very hungry.

The traveler knocked on the first door he saw. "Could you spare a little food?" he asked. The woman inside shook her head. "The harvest was poor this year," she said. "We barely have enough food from our fields for ourselves." At every house, the answer was the same, because the worried villagers had hidden their food away.

The traveler did not get angry. Instead, he calmly set his pot in the middle of the village square. He filled it with water from the well, built a small fire under it, and then dropped the gray stone into the pot.

A curious boy came closer. "What are you making?" he asked.

"Stone soup," the traveler answered. "It is the best soup in the world. Still, it would taste even better with one carrot."

The boy ran home, came back with a carrot, and dropped it into the pot. Soon other villagers gathered around to watch. "Stone soup is tasty," the traveler said as he stirred. "But a few potatoes would make it perfect."

An old farmer remembered the potatoes in his cellar. He brought a whole sack. A baker brought onions, a young girl brought a handful of beans, and someone else added salt and herbs. Each person gave just a little, but the pot grew fuller and fuller.

At last, the soup was ready, and its delicious smell filled the whole square. The villagers brought bowls and spoons and sat down together. For the first time in months, they laughed and told stories while they ate. Everyone had enough, and there was even some left over.

When the meal was over, the traveler fished the stone out of the pot. He wiped it clean and carefully put it back in his pocket.

"Wait!" called the boy. "How will we make stone soup without your magic stone?"

The traveler smiled. "The stone was never magic," he said. "The soup was made from what all of you shared."

The next morning, the traveler walked on down the road. But the villagers never forgot the lesson. From then on, they shared what they had, and no one in the village went hungry again.
stem: What is the lesson of this folktale?
choices: When everyone shares a little, there can be enough for all.
A magic stone can make delicious food.
Travelers should always carry their own food.
It is wise to hide food when times are hard.
explanation: Each villager added a small amount, and together they made a meal for everyone. The traveler says the soup came from what they shared.

Maya and her little brother, Theo, had waited all summer for this hike. Their aunt Rosa was a park ranger, and she had promised to take them to the top of Eagle Ridge. From the lookout, she said, you could see three lakes and a river shining like a silver ribbon.

They started early in the morning, and Aunt Rosa gave each of them a small backpack with water, a snack, and a whistle. She also gave Maya a compass. "Remember," she said, "the trail markers are blue. If you ever stop seeing blue, stop walking. And if you get lost, stay where you are."

For the first hour, the sky was clear and bright. Theo counted chipmunks, and Maya carefully checked the compass every time the trail turned. Then, near the top, the air grew cool, and a thick gray fog rolled over the ridge like a soft blanket. Soon Maya could barely see the trees beside the path.

"Aunt Rosa?" Theo called. His voice sounded small. Aunt Rosa had stopped to tie her boot a few steps behind them, and now the fog hid her completely.

Maya's heart was beating fast, but she remembered the safety rules. "Stay right next to me," she told Theo. She took out her whistle and blew it three times. Three short blasts meant "Come find us."

Three whistles answered from somewhere below. Maya looked at the nearest tree and discovered a blue mark painted on its trunk. "We're still on the trail," she said. "We'll stay right here by this marker so Aunt Rosa can find us."

Theo held her hand tightly, and the minutes felt like hours. At last, a tall shape came out of the fog. It was Aunt Rosa, and she was smiling.

"You did just the right thing," she said, and she hugged them both. "When you can't see, it is smart to stay put."

They waited together on a flat rock and shared their trail mix. Little by little, the sun burned through the fog, and then the gray curtain lifted, and there below them were three blue lakes and a river shining like a silver ribbon.

Theo gasped. "It was worth the wait!"

Maya smiled and tucked the compass into her pocket. She had wanted to see the view, but she was even prouder of how she had kept calm when things went wrong.

choices: A girl stays calm and follows safety rules when fog separates her from her aunt.
A park ranger teaches children how to count chipmunks.
Two children get lost because they forget their backpacks.
A family drives to a lake to go swimming.
explanation: The main events show Maya using the whistle and staying by the trail marker after the fog hides Aunt Rosa.

Have you ever seen a frog leap into a pond? That frog did not always look the way it does now. Like all animals, frogs go through a life cycle. A life cycle is the set of changes a living thing goes through as it grows. A frog's life cycle has four main stages: egg, tadpole, froglet, and adult frog.

The life cycle begins in the water. In spring, a female frog lays hundreds of eggs in a pond. The eggs are tiny black dots wrapped in clear jelly. The jelly protects the eggs and helps them stick together in a clump. Many hungry fish and birds eat frog eggs, so a frog lays a lot of them. That way, at least some will survive.

After about one to three weeks, tadpoles hatch from the eggs. A tadpole looks more like a little fish than a frog. It has a long tail for swimming and gills for breathing underwater. Tadpoles spend most of their time eating tiny plants called algae. They grow quickly.

Over the next few weeks, the tadpole begins to change in amazing ways. First, back legs start to grow. Then front legs appear. Inside its body, the tadpole grows lungs so it will be able to breathe air. Its tail gets shorter and shorter. At this stage, the young animal is called a froglet. A froglet can leave the water for short periods of time.

Finally, the tail disappears, and the froglet becomes an adult frog. For many frogs, this whole process takes three or four months. Some kinds take longer. Adult frogs have strong back legs for jumping and long sticky tongues for catching insects. They can live both in water and on land. Animals that spend part of their lives in water and part on land are called amphibians.

When the adult frog is ready, it returns to the water to lay eggs of its own. Then the life cycle starts all over again.

Scientists study frogs closely because frogs can tell us a lot about the health of a place. Frogs have thin skin that soaks up water. If a pond becomes dirty, frogs are often the first animals to get sick. A pond full of healthy frogs is usually a healthy pond.

Look up at the sky. Do you see any clouds? Clouds may look like fluffy cotton, but they are really made of billions of tiny drops of water or tiny bits of ice. Each drop is so small and light that it floats in the air.

How do clouds form? It all starts with the sun. The sun warms water in oceans, lakes, and even puddles. Some of the water turns into an invisible gas called water vapor. You cannot see it, but it is all around you. This change is called evaporation. The warm water vapor rises high into the sky, where the air is much colder. The cold air cools the vapor, and it changes back into tiny drops of water. This change is called condensation. When billions of these drops crowd together, they form a cloud.

Clouds come in different shapes, and each shape has a name. Cumulus clouds are big, white, and puffy. They often look like piles of cotton balls. On a sunny day, cumulus clouds usually mean nice weather. But if they grow very tall and dark, a thunderstorm might be on the way.

Stratus clouds are flat and gray. They spread across the sky like a blanket and can hide the sun all day. Stratus clouds often bring light rain. Fog is really a stratus cloud that forms close to the ground.

Cirrus clouds are thin and wispy. They float very high in the sky, where it is so cold that they are made of ice instead of water drops. Cirrus clouds often look like white feathers. They can be a sign that the weather will change in a day or two.

So why does rain fall from clouds? Inside a cloud, the tiny drops bump into each other and join together. Little by little, they grow bigger and heavier. When the drops become too heavy to float, they fall to the ground as rain. If the air is cold enough, they fall as snow instead.

Weather scientists study clouds to help them tell what the weather will be. You can be a weather watcher, too. The next time you go outside, look up. The clouds may be telling you what kind of day is coming.

About two hundred years ago, the United States was a young country. Many families were moving west to start farms. But there was a big problem. There were no trains or highways yet. Roads were rough and muddy, and wagons moved very slowly. It could take weeks to send a load of wheat from the farms in the West to New York City. It cost a lot of money, too.

A man named DeWitt Clinton had an idea. He wanted to build a canal across the state of New York. A canal is a waterway that people dig across land so that boats can travel on it. Clinton's canal would join Lake Erie in the west to the Hudson River in the east. Then boats could carry goods all the way from the Great Lakes to New York City.

Many people thought the plan was foolish. They made fun of it and called it "Clinton's Ditch." The canal would need to be 363 miles long! Still, Clinton did not give up. In 1817, after he became governor of New York, workers began to dig.

The work was very hard. Thousands of workers dug with shovels and picks. Horses helped them move dirt and rock. The land had hills and valleys, so the workers built locks. A lock is like a water elevator. It raises or lowers a boat so that it can move to a higher or lower part of the canal.

In 1825, after eight years of work, the Erie Canal was finally done. Flat boats called barges floated on the water. Mules and horses walked on a path beside the canal and pulled the barges with long ropes.

The canal changed the country. Shipping goods became much faster and much cheaper. Farmers could sell their crops in faraway cities. Towns along the canal, such as Buffalo and Rochester, grew into busy cities. New York City became one of the most important ports in the world.

Today, trucks and trains carry most goods, but the Erie Canal is still open. Now people ride in small boats or bike along the old path to enjoy the view. The canal that people once called a foolish ditch helped a young nation grow.
